title: The Lotus in the Lake
iast: tasmin magnaṃ gaṇaka kathaya kṣipram ambhaḥ-pramāṇam ||
translation: In a pond whose water was crowded with cakravāka and krauñca birds, the tip of a lotus bud was seen standing one span (half a hasta) above the water. Struck by the wind, it moved slowly, slowly, and went under the water at a distance of two hastas. O mathematician, tell quickly the depth of the water.
translation_hi: चकवा और क्रौंच पक्षियों से भरे एक तालाब में पानी के ऊपर एक कमल की कली का सिरा एक बित्ता (आधा हाथ) ऊँचा दिखाई दिया। हवा के झोंके से वह धीरे धीरे हिला और दो हाथ की दूरी पर पानी में डूब गया। हे गणितज्ञ, जल्दी बताओ कि पानी कितना गहरा है?

words.note: cakra = cakravāka (ruddy shelduck), krauñca = crane. A dvandva ('and') compound.
Locative of taḍāga. Hindi तालाब comes from this family.
Ablative of toya (water). त् → द् before a vowel: तोयादूर्ध्वम्.

words.meaning: the tip of a lotus bud

words.note: Repetition for emphasis. Compare Hindi धीरे धीरे.
yugma = pair. Locative: 'at a pair of hastas' (distance).
Past participle of √majj (to sink). Hindi मग्न (absorbed).

grammar: Consonant sandhi: तोयात् + ऊर्ध्वम् → तोयादूर्ध्वम्. A final त् becomes द् before a vowel.
Long vowel sandhi: अनिलेन + आहतम् → अनिलेनाहतम्, क्व + अपि → क्वापि.
Instrumental case: अनिलेन 'by the wind'. The instrumental marks the agent or the means.
Vocative: गणक 'O mathematician!' Bhaskara speaks directly to you, the reader.
Meter: Mandākrāntā means 'slowly stepping'. Its slow, heavy rhythm matches मन्दं मन्दम्, the lotus moving slowly in the wind.
question: What is the depth of the water, in hastas?
solution:
Let the depth be d. The full stalk is d + ½. When the wind pushes it over, the same stalk becomes the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides d and 2:

(d + ½)² = d² + 2²  ⟹  d² + d + ¼ = d² + 4  ⟹  d = 3¾ hastas

General rule: d = (b² − h²) / (2h) = (4 − ¼) / 1 = 3.75

If a hasta is taken as about 45 cm, the pond is roughly 1.7 m deep.

Science link: the same geometry is used in physics to find how far a pendulum or a moored buoy shifts sideways when a force tilts it. Chinese mathematicians posed a reed-in-a-pond problem centuries earlier in the Nine Chapters, so this puzzle connects Indian and world mathematics.
